title: Balls: 40mm plastic, stars and why the ball changed
seo_title: Table tennis balls explained: 40mm, plastic and stars
description: How table tennis balls work: the 40mm size and 2.7g weight, why celluloid gave way to plastic, what 40+ and the star ratings mean and which balls to buy.
summary: Every competition ball is 40mm across, weighs 2.7g and is now made of plastic. Here is how the ball got that way, what the markings mean and which to buy for practice and matches.
key_points: The rules say the ball is 40mm across, weighs 2.7g, is made of plastic and is white or orange with a matt finish.
The 40mm ball replaced the 38mm ball in international events from 1 October 2000.
Plastic replaced celluloid at ITTF events from 1 July 2014, mainly because celluloid is highly flammable.
"40+" on the stamp marks a plastic ball; three stars marks a maker's top grade, the one used for matches.
For leagues and tournaments in England the ball must be a brand and type approved by the ITTF.
body: A table tennis ball is a hollow plastic sphere 40mm across, weighing 2.7g, in white or orange with a matt finish. That is what the laws require, and every match ball you will see on television meets it. The 40mm size dates from 2000 and the plastic from 2014. The stars printed on the box are a maker's quality grade: three stars means a ball fit for matches.
## What the rules say

The laws of table tennis, written by the International Table Tennis Federation (ITTF), give the ball three lines. Law 2.3 says it must be spherical with a diameter of 40mm, weigh 2.7g, and be "made of plastic material", "white or orange, and matt".

The ITTF's ball manual, which sets out how balls are tested for approval, turns those numbers into tolerances. A single ball must measure between 40.00mm and 40.55mm and weigh between 2.67g and 2.77g. It must be round to within 0.24mm, and when dropped from 305mm on to a steel block it must bounce back between 240mm and 265mm. A ball may have at most one seam, the join where two halves meet, and that seam must be smooth.
## From 38mm to 40mm

For most of the sport's history the ball was smaller. It had been a maximum of 38mm since the ITTF first codified the laws in 1928. The 40mm ball replaced it in ITTF international events from 1 October 2000, and the Sydney 2000 Olympics were the last major event played with the old ball.

The bigger ball was meant to make the game easier to watch and to play. In 2000 the ITTF president at the time, Adham Sharara, cited tests showing the 40mm ball was 3% to 8% slower, 3% to 6% less spinny and 11% to 16% more visible. Timo Boll, who made his Olympic debut that year, has said the bigger ball "made it harder to put the same rotation" on it.
## From celluloid to plastic

For decades balls were made of celluloid, an early plastic that is highly flammable. That made celluloid hard to produce, store and ship: most countries had stopped making it, and celluloid balls could not be carried on aircraft. From 1 July 2014 all ITTF sanctioned and world title events switched to balls made of other plastics. The first international event to use them was the Belarus Open on the World Tour in August 2014, and the first World Championships were in Suzhou in 2015.

To tell the two apart, plastic balls carry "40+" on the stamp, while celluloid balls carried "40" alone. Boll said the plastic ball "cut down the rotation". In 2014 only ITTF events had to switch: other competitions were free to choose which ball to use.

The material is still changing. In 2025 the ITTF approved a ball made with 65% recycled plastic, the DHS RS40+, which made its international debut that August at Europe Smash, the WTT Grand Smash in Malmö.
## What the stars mean

Stars are not set out in the laws. They are a grade the maker prints on the ball after its own final inspection. According to the ITTF ball manual, balls that pass are stamped with the approved quality mark, for example three stars, while those that fall short are stamped with one or two stars.

In practice that gives you two kinds of ball. Three-star balls are the ones used in matches and are the most consistent in size, roundness and bounce. One- and two-star balls are cheaper and fine for practice, especially when you are hitting hundreds of balls in a drill or with a coach.
## Seamed and seamless balls

Most balls are made in two halves joined at a seam. Some makers also produce seamless balls, formed in one piece. Both are allowed, but the ITTF treats them as different products, so a seamless ball must be sold under its own brand or product name. The manual also sets a slightly different hardness range for seamless balls.
## Which ball for which match

For a game at home or in the park, any ball that bounces properly will do. For league and tournament play in England, Table Tennis England's byelaws add a rule to the laws: the ball "shall be of a brand and type currently approved by the ITTF". Look for the ITTF approval mark on the ball or the box.

You will rarely have to choose. Your league or the home club normally supplies the ball. Its colour matters for what you wear: under the ITTF regulations, the main colour of your shirt and shorts must be clearly different from the ball's. At international events players can pick a ball before the match from those specified for the competition, but they "shall not choose balls in the playing area". If they cannot agree, the umpire takes one at random from the box.
## Buying balls

Buy three-star plastic balls marked 40+ for matches and serious practice, and a bigger box of training balls for drills and multiball, where a coach feeds balls quickly one after another. If you know which ball your league uses, practise with the same one. Throw away cracked balls.
